author: H. K. Justice
title: Minnesota Legislature approves excavation notice system overhaul; awaits governor's action - St. Cloud Sun
text:
Legislation spearheaded by State Sen. Jeff R. Howe is set to reform Minnesota’s excavation notice system by introducing electronic responses, improved facility marking protocols, and updated standards for records of underground infrastructure, according to Minnesota State Legislature.
The measure passed both legislative chambers and was forwarded to the governor on May 20, 2026, securing a 133-0 vote in the House and a 64-0 vote in the Senate.
Billed as SF4339 and introduced on March 11, 2026, during the 94th Legislature’s regular session, the legislation’s official description addresses modified requirements for excavation notification systems and the addition of electronic positive responses.
The summary below is derived from the full bill text and may be paraphrased for clarity.
The statute changes will require operators to submit electronic confirmation of facility locate statuses for excavation or boundary survey requests, with the notification center relaying this information to excavators. Facility operators are directed to mark underground utility locations without charge and identify any abandoned infrastructure they maintain. Standards for visual marks are set out, in addition to requirements for regular, accurate recordkeeping. From 2026, new or abandoned facility projects must include as-built records using geospatial technology, aside from certain small operators. The statute revisions will take effect Aug. 1, 2026, while updated contact information requirements begin Jan. 1, 2027.
Among House members, 66 Democrats joined 67 Republicans in favor of passage.
On the Senate side, support came from 33 Democrats and 31 Republicans.
The principal author, Sen. Jeff R. Howe (Republican-13th District), filed the bill alongside co-sponsors Sen. John A. Hoffman (Democrat-34th District) and Rep. Larry Kraft (Democrat-46th District).
Howe earned his degree from Saint Cloud State University.
A Republican, Howe was elected to the Minnesota State Senate in 2018 to represent the 13th district, following the tenure of state senator Michelle Fischbach.
According to Minnesota’s legislative process, bills are introduced in either the House or Senate before being assigned to committees for consideration and possible revision. Supported bills continue to a vote by the full chamber. Agreement by both chambers sends a bill to the governor, who may sign it, veto it, or allow it to become law without signature. Sessions are held yearly, starting in January, with legislators proposing thousands of bills, a limited portion of which become law.
